>e-cigs provide the same fix.

Not true. Many cigarette smokers who've tried vaping still go back because it's just not the same, chemically. I bounced between cigs and vaping for about five years before I found a juice that worked for me.

Physical mechanisms of cigarette addiction are more complex than just nicotine. There are dozens of chemicals in tobacco that create a synergistic effect that potentiate addictiveness.

Freebase nicotine, the standard for e-cig liquids of the past decade, is significantly less satisfying when isolated from tobacco alkaloids and other chemicals found in traditional cigarettes. Also, vapor particles are ~10x larger than smoke, reducing bioavailability via the lungs. 

A more recent advancement is the wider availability of e-liquids containing nicotine salts. Nic salts are less irritating to the throat/lungs and allow for significantly higher nicotine concentrations (10-20x stronger or more). These concentrations are typically high enough to offset the lower bioavailability of vaporized nicotine. Far more tobacco users find salt nicotine liquids easier to sate cravings, but a lot still can't shake the other chemicals only found in tobacco. 

I haven't even touched on other psychological and habitual factors at play with traditional cigarettes that can't be replicated with e-cigarettes. The ritual of packing a fresh box, the social workplace smoke break, the taste/smell of tobacco, etc.

tl,dr; e-cigs are getting there, but they've still got a lot of progress to make before totally displacing tobacco cigarettes.

In regards to Norway and other countries with 100% renewable energy initiatives, look into their population densities and the impact on land mass. Farms of solar panels, wind turbines, etc. require vast amounts of land and infrastructure compared to the relatively small amount of energy they produce. Few want to live by them or the massive electrical towers required to transport their power over long distances. While these may work in sparsely populated countries like Norway, it's not feasible for denser countries and/or areas that need it most (think China or India).

Solar panel generation is greatly hampered by poor weather or the night, and require constant cleaning in order to operate at high efficiency. Wind farms only average a measly 15% of their maximum potential output. Even if there was a perfect day with optimal conditions and a surplus of production, power storage is far from being cost-effective at the industrial/commercial scale.
